title: Snare drum
reference_instrument: Salamander Drumkit snare, 14x6, wires on, overhead microphones (Alexander Holm, CC BY-SA 3.0); the kit copies its sizes, not its materials. The distribution holds one overhead-labelled sample set and does not say whether close-microphone signal is mixed into it, so a line balance measured on it may not be comparable to an overhead-only render
summary: A 14x6 snare from fs-vkplate's one finite-difference solver. It has two tensioned PET heads from a sourced film card, the air between them, a hickory stick from a sourced wood card, and eighteen snare strands pressed up into the resonant head. On the card route each strand is a helical coil of steel music wire. Its geometry is the maker's stated wire diameter, coil outer diameter and pitch, and its stiffness, mass and loss come from two steel cards and the air, not from a recording. The strands' count, spacing and length are declared. Their tension, preload and contact law were adopted in a kit retuning graded against the recording (96ccf8f1b) and are still in use. The strand ends are pinned with no damping, so the lowest coil modes keep their long material decay. These figures were measured on 2026-10-31 on the 3.5 mm grid (the site render) and the 2.5 mm grid, both with every strand node on the head node it presses (02b7d8b17). Over the first 250 ms against the recording, the 125 Hz band is 4.8 and 7.5 dB louder, the 63 Hz band is 1.3 dB quieter and 2.6 dB louder, and the bands from 1 to 8 kHz are 7 to 11 dB weaker. The spectral centroid is 353 and 338 Hz against the recording's 1083 Hz, and the share of energy above 1 kHz is 2.7 and 3.4 % against 21 %. The two grids agree, so the missing high band is not a grid artifact. The buzz ends too early on both grids: the 2 to 16 kHz band is 30 dB below its maximum at 100 ms, against 235 ms in the recording. It holds to the recording for about 60 ms, then falls about 25 dB in 40 ms to near the recording's wires-off level; the recording has no such fall. The cause is not named. At half and double the strike speed the band reaches 30 dB down at 212 and 178 ms, later in both cases, so a single lift-off threshold does not explain it. The presets, the live engine and the GPU renderer keep the older plain-string wires, which were fitted to a recording and are labelled so.
physics_present: Batter and resonant heads: tensioned PET film with its own bending stiffness and Berger nonlinearity, from a sourced film card
The exterior radiation load of each head from a baked baffled table, and the viscous boundary layer of the air on both faces of each head
A lumped adiabatic air cavity between the heads, and a radiation resistance on their net volume flow
A hickory stick from a sourced wood card, with a Hertz tip transversely isotropic about the grain

Snare strands on the card route: coils whose bending stiffness combines wire bending and wire torsion over each turn, and whose mass is the wire's, from the steel music-wire card and a spring-moduli card for the shear modulus

Per-mode loss of each coil: the computed thermoelastic loss of the round wire, the card's measured excess bending loss inside its measured band, and the exact linear air drag across and along the wire
One-sided power-law contacts between every strand node and the resonant head, each solved implicitly
A Rayleigh-integral microphone about a metre away, with a floor reflection
physics_missing: Strand-end supports: each strand is pinned at the end plates with no strand-end or cord damping, so the lowest coil modes keep their long material decay. Against the recording the 63 and 125 Hz bands are 2.6 and 7.5 dB louder on the 2.5 mm grid, and 1.3 dB quieter and 4.8 dB louder on the 3.5 mm grid

Convergence below 2.5 mm: at 4.5 m/s the 3.5 and 2.5 mm grids agree on when the buzz ends, on each octave's 20 dB fall from 500 Hz to 8 kHz, and on the centroid within 4 %; the 125 Hz band moves 2.8 dB. A 2.0 mm grid has not been run

What ends the buzz: not the grid, and not a single lift-off threshold. At 4.5 and 9 m/s the drum's lowest band (100 to 180 Hz) collapses first and the buzz follows about 25 ms later; at 2.25 m/s that band does not collapse. In the recording it falls at the same rate at two dynamics, and the buzz outlasts it. All strands share one declared preload and one declared contact loss

The resonant head is heard only through the floor image, not directly. A lumped estimate of both heads and the air between them (pexfp.378, parked) says: if this estimate is right, the current renders overstate each drum's lowest line by 13-17 dB at the overhead
Per-strand tension and preload: one tension and one preload serve every strand. Neither is sourced: both, with the contact law, were adopted in a kit retuning graded against the recording (96ccf8f1b)
The strand count, spacing and length are declared estimates, and the strand-to-head contact law is the retuned one
Wire torsion loss is unmeasured and omitted. The air drag is the linear law, which understates the drag on a rattling wire. The wires' loss is therefore a lower bound
Head film and edge loss: the film card makes no audio-band loss claim, so both are stated unknowns entered as zero
Shell, hoop and rim vibration, and the cavity's own acoustic modes (the cavity is lumped)
The snare is simulated alone, so it does not buzz when another drum is struck
On the preset, live and GPU routes the strands are plain strings fitted to a recording (96ccf8f1b), not physics
